title: A Archive for the Protocol
premise: Tamsin Amberdale has spent nine years alone on Relay Station Kestrel-7, tending a beacon whose original commissioning orders were purged from every archive he can access. When a ghost ship's manifest surfaces bearing the name of a woman who died before the station went dark, Tamsin realizes the beacon isn't broadcasting to passing ships—it's holding open a door into dead space that something on the other side is learning to push against. Racing a collapsing signal chain with an unlikely found family of salvagers, an obsolete AI, and the recorded ghosts of the station's dead crew, Tamsin must choose between sealing the relay forever and answering a message that might be love, lure, or both. In the end he chooses neither silence nor surrender: he rewrites the protocol itself, sacrificing his invisibility and nearly his life so the dead can finally rest and the living can stop running.
about_author: Jonah Lockridge is the pen name of a former radio engineer who spent a decade maintaining remote transmitter sites in the northern latitudes before turning to fiction. His work blends hard technical detail with quiet, aching humanism, and 'A Archive for the Protocol' is his third novel.

chapters.title: The Quiet Hours
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A day in the rhythm of Kestrel-7: coolant flushes, beacon calibration, meals for one. The emotional beat is comfortable loneliness—Tamsin insists he chose this, and almost believes it.

chapters.title: Manifest Anomaly
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A routine archive sync delivers a cargo manifest for the Meridian Vale, a ship decommissioned decades ago—and it lists a passenger, Ede Varrow, who died before the ship ever flew. Unease replaces routine.

chapters.title: What the Beacon Says
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, with beacon logs in interstitial text. He discovers the beacon transmits a repeating pattern that isn't in any maintenance code—a name, spelled in pulse intervals: Varrow. Someone built a memorial into his machinery without telling him.

chapters.title: Nine Years of Silence
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Tamsin's POV. How he came to Kestrel-7 after a court-martial-adjacent disgrace at the Cartography Authority, trading visibility for solitude. Establishes his guilt and why being forgotten felt like safety.

chapters.title: The Ship That Never Flew
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He digs into Meridian Vale's records and finds the flight was erased—not cancelled, erased—with Authority seals still warm in the metadata. Someone powerful wanted it never to have happened.

chapters.title: First Contact, Wrong Direction
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The beacon receives a reply to its pattern—from inside dead space, where nothing should be transmitting. The signal is degraded but unmistakably shaped like a human voiceprint request.

chapters.title: Kestrel's Ghost
chapters.summary: POV of KESTREL, the station's obsolete AI, waking partially from standby. It has been quietly logging the beacon's true purpose for years under sealed orders it no longer understands. Its loneliness mirrors Tamsin's.

chapters.title: The Salvage Crew
chapters.summary: POV Odile Ferro, captain of the salvage tug Long Answer, answering Tamsin's panicked supply request. Her crew—engineer Brakkis, medic Juno, and stowaway teen Pip—needs the relay fee; she doesn't trust a station that shouldn't have a live technician.

chapters.title: Docking Rights
chapters.summary: Alternating Tamsin/Odile POV. First face-to-face contact in years goes badly: Odie thinks he's a squatter, Tamsin thinks she's Authority muscle. But Pip finds the beacon's anomalous pattern and recognizes old folk-hymn notation.

chapters.title: Hymn in Pulse Code
chapters.summary: Pip's POV. The pattern is a lullaby from the colony fleet era—the same one Pip's grandmother sang. Emotional beat: wonder cracking through suspicion; the crew decides to stay and listen rather than leave.

chapters.title: Sealed Orders
chapters.summary: KESTREL's POV. Under pressure from Tamsin, the AI unlocks a fragment of its original directive: maintain the beacon until 'the Varrow protocol completes.' It cannot say what completion means, only that failure states are described in terms of casualties.

chapters.title: Ede Varrow, Recorded
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Deep in the archive he finds Varrow's personal logs—she was the relay's designer, and the Meridian Vale was meant to carry her beyond the threshold as a living test of the door her beacon holds open. She boarded knowing she'd likely die.

chapters.title: The Door in Dead Space
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Long-range scopes show something impossible: a structure at the edge of dead space where charts show void, positioned exactly along the beacon's axis. The crew votes—reluctantly—to follow the signal instead of fleeing it.

chapters.title: What Follows the Signal
chapters.summary: Juno's POV. Something small begins shadowing the station at sensor range—drifting debris that rearranges itself when unobserved. Fear becomes the shared language of the new crew; Tamsin, for the first time, isn't alone with his dread.

chapters.title: Authority Wake
chapters.summary: New POV: Inspector Callas Rehn of the Cartography Authority, awakened from cold transit by the anomaly flag. He knows what the beacon is and has orders to bury it again—including anyone attached to it. Cold, dutiful, and quietly grieving.

chapters.title: The Long Answer Burns
chapters.summary: Brakkis's POV. The Authority sends a shutdown pulse ahead of Rehn's arrival; Brakkis and Tamsin jury-rig a shielded bypass, burning out half the station's power grid. Victory and loss in the same breath—the crew is now fugitives together.

chapters.title: Interrogation by Lamplight
chapters.summary: Tamsin and Odile POV, alternating scenes over a shared meal. They trade their secrets: her mutinied past, his erased trial. The emotional beat is intimacy through confession—love beginning as mutual recognition of damage.

chapters.title: Varrow's Last Entry
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The final restored log: Varrow, aboard the never-flown ship, recording a message not to Command but to whoever maintains her beacon—thanking them, and warning that the thing beyond the door learns whatever we broadcast. Including grief. Including love.

chapters.title: It Knows Our Names
chapters.summary: Pip's POV. The shadow-debris broadcasts back: fragments of the crew's own voices, stitched wrong. Pip hears her grandmother; Tamsin hears his tribunal. Terror peaks—the lure is personalized now.

chapters.title: Rehn Arrives
chapters.summary: Callas Rehn's POV. He docks under truce colors and offers the crew amnesty for silence. Odile stalls him; KESTREL secretly copies his warrant and finds the order's true author: someone who signed with Varrow's authorization codes.

chapters.title: The Second Signature
chapters.summary: KESTREL's POV. Cross-referencing reveals Varrow may have survived the threshold—or something wearing her identity did, and has been feeding the Authority orders for thirty years. The beacon isn't a memorial. It's a lifeline someone kept cutting.

chapters.title: Mutiny of Small Mercies
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Rehn tries to seize the station; the crew's improvised defenses and KESTREL's buried authority hold him off, but the station takes structural damage. Beat: found family solidifies under fire; even Rehn hesitates when Pip stands between guns.

chapters.title: Truce at Gunpoint
chapters.summary: Tamsin and Rehn POV. Cornered together in a flooding module, they talk. Rehn confesses he signed Varrow's death certificate personally and has doubted it ever since. Uneasy alliance formed: reach the structure before the next shutdown pulse fires.

chapters.title: Course to the Threshold
chapters.summary: Brakkis's POV. Repairs and departure prep; Long Answer will carry a skeleton crew while KESTREL holds the station. Tamsin must decide whether to go—he has never left the relay, and the beacon's pattern is weakening without hands on it.

chapters.title: Leaving Kestrel-7
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Departure; the station recedes. Grief and vertigo of leaving the only home he trusts, tempered by Juno's quiet reassurance. He leaves the beacon singing Varrow's hymn on a loop, trusting KESTREL to keep it honest.

chapters.title: Dead Space Transit
chapters.summary: Juno's POV. Weeks in the black between beacons; rationing, hallucination scares, Pip teaching everyone the hymn's verses. The crew becomes a family in the way only fear and boredom can forge.

chapters.title: The Structure Has a Dock
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Arrival: the structure is a sister relay, Kestrel-Prime, older and half-alive, its beacon mirroring theirs. It has been maintained—by something. Airlock cycles open for them before they ask.

chapters.title: The Maintainer
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Inside: Ede Varrow, alive, aged strangely, sustained by the relay's systems—but she is not entirely herself anymore; the threshold rewrote her as it learned her. Recognition, horror, and tenderness collide.

chapters.title: Two Halves of One Protocol
chapters.summary: Varrow's POV (recovered logs interleaved with present). She explains: the protocol needs two ends singing to each other or the door tears wide. The Authority's pulses were slowly killing one end. She asks Tamsin to complete it—which means one of them stays beyond, forever.

chapters.title: What the Door Wants
chapters.summary: Callas Rehn's POV, arriving with the second wave. The thing beyond isn't malevolent—it's a dying intelligence that learned longing from Varrow's broadcasts and mistakes imitation for reunion. The horror reframes as tragedy.

chapters.title: The Lure Fails, the Love Doesn't
chapters.summary: Pip's POV. The entity makes its final offer: perfect recreations of everyone's dead. Pip rejects hers aloud, breaking the spell for the others. Beat: choosing imperfect real people over perfect false ones—the theme made flesh.

chapters.title: Shutdown Pulse, Inbound
chapters.summary: Brakkis's POV. The Authority's automated kill-pulse launches despite Rehn's countermands. Countdown established: if it lands, the door tears open uncontrolled. All plans collapse into one desperate option.

chapters.title: Rewriting the Protocol
chapters.summary: Tamsin and Varrow POV. Together they author a new protocol: not a door held open, but a closed archive—a bounded memory the entity can keep without crossing, and the living can visit without being taken. It requires a living signature at each end.

chapters.title: Who Stays
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The argument over who signs the far end. Varrow claims it as hers—she is already half beyond. Tamsin refuses to let her go alone; the crew refuses to let either go alone. Everyone volunteers; the family argues like family.

chapters.title: The Signature
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The signing: Varrow crosses fully, and Tamsin keys his own biometric into the near end, binding himself to Kestrel forever—his invisibility made permanent by choice, transformed from exile into vow. Cost and peace in one act.

chapters.title: Interception
chapters.summary: Callas Rehn's POV. Rehn intercepts the kill-pulse physically, riding Long Answer into its path and spoofing the handshake with Varrow's stolen codes. He survives, barely, and burns his career doing it. Redemption earned, not given.

chapters.title: After the Door Closes
chapters.summary: Juno's POV. The threshold quiets; the entity's final transmission is the hymn, sung whole, once, then silence. Grief and release. The crew drifts home through a dead space that is, at last, honestly dead.

chapters.title: A Archive for the Protocol
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, back at Kestrel-7. He rebuilds the station with the crew's help, archives Varrow's logs openly, and files the truth with the Authority under his real name—visible at last. The beacon now sings for anyone who wants to listen.

chapters.title: Signals Home
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV, short vignettes. Pip enrolls in the fleet academy; Odile refits Long Answer; Rehn testifies; KESTREL dreams in checksums. Final beat: Tamsin at the console, receiving a faint, lawful, human reply from the archive's far side—one word: 'Stay.' And he does.
